title: Police officer never knew assailant was mentally challenged, inquest told
article: The police officer who shot and killed Douglas Minty had no way of knowing that he suffered from any mental issues, a coroner's court heard Wednesday.

Minty, a 59-year-old Elmvale resident, was a developmentally challenged man who was shot five times after he advanced toward the officer with a kitchen knife in the driveway of his home on June 22, 2009.
But OPP Const. Graham Seguin had no way of knowing Minty had either mental or emotional issues.
The incident began when Minty got into a physical altercation with a door-to-door water heater salesman who came to his mother's Lawson Avenue home, where Minty lived.
The salesman called police after Minty punched him in the face.

After speaking with the salesman, a police dispatcher made the call to Seguin, but there was no mention of mental disability. There were no red flags, no criminal record, no history of violence or issues surrounding the home address.
Two police officers were dispatched, but Seguin was first on the scene.

On the witness stand, OPP training co-ordinator Sgt. Nathalie Rivard agreed it was only "common sense" and Seguin was performing his "duty to investigate," when he got out of his cruiser alone to speak with the complainant and then with Minty, who was standing in his driveway.
As Minty approached the officer bearing a small kitchen knife, Seguin repeatedly ordered him to "drop the weapon," but Minty continued toward him.
Seguin fired five shots and minutes later, Minty lay dead on the street.

Rivard told the jury that OPP policy states whenever there is a concern of mental or emotional illness, two police officers must attend. If one officer arrives first, that officer must wait until the other officer arrives - unless there is a danger that requires immediate intervention.
"But police officers are not doctors, they are not psychiatrists, they are not psychologists, correct?" asked the Seguin's lawyer, Andrew McKay.
"That's correct," answered Rivard.
"So if they can't recognize the situation they are not going to be able to apply that policy, correct?" McKay asked.
"That's correct," answered Rivard.
She added no amount of training would prepare a police officer in future similar situations - if the information isn't given to the officer.
The dispatcher who relayed the call is expected to testify on Thursday.

The inquest jury will not determine guilt or innocence, but rather will examine the circumstances surrounding Minty's death and will consider police response to individuals who are developmentally delayed.
The jury may make recommendations aimed at preventing similar deaths.
Outside court, Minty family lawyer Julian Roy said the family is hoping for answers.

"We don't know if Mr. Minty would be alive today if things were done differently," Roy said. "The family wants to know what happened, and most of all, the family wants to ensure this tragedy never happens again."
